units.title: Unit 15 — Countryside
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 34–35 (PDF pages 38–39).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Travel and the environment · countryside, landscape and tourism
learningObjectives: Describe rural environments using precise adjective–noun collocations and natural landscape verbs.
Use expressions for noticing sights, ruins, rivers and views, including correct verb–noun pairings.
Describe tourist scenery and beaches while distinguishing view, landscape, countryside and scenery.
Recognise register and figurative meanings in expressions such as well worth seeing and dominate the landscape.

items.pt: região rural ao redor; arredores campestres
items.example: From the hilltop, we could see the surrounding countryside for miles.
items.note: Surrounding refers to the land around a particular town, building or place.

items.example: After years abroad, she was delighted to see the familiar landscape again.
items.note: A landscape that you recognise from past experience; familiar refers to recognition, not necessarily beauty.

items.example: The village lies in a gentle landscape of low hills and farmland.
items.note: Gentle describes scenery without steep, dramatic or threatening features.

items.example: The road crossed open fields before reaching the forest.
items.note: Open fields have few trees, buildings or other obstructions.

items.pt: paisagem desolada; paisagem árida e sombria
items.example: The abandoned mine stood in a bleak landscape of bare rock.
items.note: Bleak suggests an exposed, unattractive or harsh-looking environment.

items.example: The trail became steeper as we approached the rocky mountains.
items.note: Rocky describes terrain with many exposed stones or rock formations.

items.pt: seguir uma trilha; seguir um caminho
items.example: We decided to follow a path through the valley rather than climb the hill.
items.note: Follow a path means move along its course; use follow, not accompany, here.

items.pt: virar uma esquina; fazer uma curva
items.example: As we turned a corner, the lake suddenly appeared ahead of us.
items.note: The phrase works for both streets and turns in paths.

items.example: I managed to catch a glimpse of a deer before it disappeared into the trees.
items.note: A glimpse is a brief, often accidental sighting; catch is the conventional verb.

items.example: Could you take a picture of the waterfall from this side?
items.note: Take a picture and take a photo are both natural expressions; do a picture is not natural for photography.

items.example: We caught sight of the lighthouse just before sunset.
items.note: Catch sight of means suddenly notice or see something, often after looking for it.

items.pt: fazer uma curva; contornar uma curva
items.example: The cyclists rounded a bend and found a steep climb ahead.
items.note: Round a bend is a natural way to describe movement around a curve in a road or path.

items.pt: entrar no campo de visão; aparecer à vista
items.example: The old bridge came into view as the train left the tunnel.
items.note: Something comes into view when it becomes visible, rather than necessarily moving itself.

items.example: Without repairs, the abandoned farmhouse may fall into ruin.
items.note: Buildings fall into ruin when they deteriorate over a long period. Fell into ruin is the past form.

items.example: The ancient fortress still lies in ruins above the village.
items.note: Lie in ruins describes the current ruined state of a building or site.

items.pt: vale muito a pena conhecer; merece ser visto
items.example: The small botanical garden is well worth seeing in spring.
items.note: Well worth is followed by an -ing form, not by an infinitive.

items.pt: cenário impressionante; localização de grande impacto visual
items.example: The monastery occupies a dramatic setting above the cliffs.
items.note: Setting refers to the surrounding location and its visual effect, not a theatre stage.

items.example: The sheep grazed on a steep slope behind the farm.
items.note: Steep indicates a sharp incline or decline.

items.example: A fast-flowing river separates the village from the national park.
items.note: The compound adjective fast-flowing describes the speed of moving water.

items.pt: montanhas se erguem imponentes acima do vale
items.example: Snowy mountains tower above the quiet valley.
items.note: Tower above is a figurative use of tower meaning rise very high relative to surroundings.

items.pt: região rural preservada; paisagem campestre intocada
items.example: The region is known for its unspoilt countryside and quiet villages.
items.note: Unspoilt means largely unaffected by development or damage; British spelling is unspoilt.

items.pt: borda da floresta; limite da mata
items.example: We found a campsite near the edge of the forest.
items.note: The edge of a forest is its boundary; the source presents a cottage located on the edge of dense woodland.

items.example: Very little sunlight reaches the ground in this dense forest.
items.note: Dense describes trees growing close together.

items.pt: obstruir a vista; bloquear a visão
items.example: A row of new buildings will block the view of the sea.
items.note: Block the view means obstruct what someone can see; jam the view is incorrect.

items.example: We photographed the snow-covered mountains from the train.
items.note: Snow-covered is a hyphenated compound adjective when used before a noun.

items.word: a stream winds through the forest
items.example: A stream winds through the forest before joining the main river.
items.note: Wind is pronounced /waɪnd/ as a verb meaning follow a twisting route, not like the noun for moving air.

items.pt: destruir o ambiente rural; devastar a paisagem campestre
items.example: Uncontrolled development could destroy the countryside around the lake.
items.note: Destroy expresses severe damage, rather than a small alteration to the landscape.

items.example: Residents formed a group to protect the environment around the wetlands.
items.note: Protect combines with the environment to describe preventing damage to natural surroundings.

items.example: A chain of mountains runs along the eastern border.
items.note: Chain of mountains describes a connected mountain range; established in the unit correction exercise.

items.example: A river flows slowly across the plain before reaching the coast.
items.note: Flow is natural for the movement of water; dance is inappropriate in this factual description.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: The cabin offers uninterrupted views across the valley.
items.note: Uninterrupted means that trees or buildings do not block the line of sight.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: Visitors can enjoy a panoramic view from the observation tower.
items.note: A panoramic view covers a very wide area, not just a close-up view.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: There is a spectacular view of the coastline from the cliffs.
items.note: Spectacular emphasises strong visual impact or beauty.

items.pt: admirar a paisagem; contemplar a vista
items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: We stopped at the lookout point to admire the view.
items.note: Admire combines naturally with view when taking time to appreciate scenery.

items.pt: apreciar a vista; desfrutar da paisagem
items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: We sat on the terrace to enjoy the view of the harbour.
items.note: Enjoy the view focuses on the pleasure of looking at scenery.

items.pt: paisagem de tirar o fôlego; cenários deslumbrantes
items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: The national park is famous for its breathtaking scenery.
items.note: Breathtaking expresses exceptionally impressive natural beauty.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: The volcanic peak dominates the landscape around the town.
items.note: A prominent object dominates the landscape when it is the main visible feature.

items.pt: uma praia se estende por quilômetros
items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: A beach stretches for miles along the southern coast.
items.note: Stretch describes something extending over a long distance; reach for miles is not the target expression.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: The children spent the afternoon playing on a sandy beach.
items.note: Sandy describes a beach covered in sand; sanded beach is not the natural phrase.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: We found a secluded beach away from the main tourist areas.
items.note: Secluded means sheltered or not easily reached, usually with few people.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: The island is known for its golden sands and clear water.
items.note: A descriptive tourism expression for beaches with golden-coloured sand.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: They moved to the peaceful countryside to escape city noise.
items.note: Peaceful emphasises quiet surroundings and little disturbance.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: A short drive takes you into the tranquil countryside.
items.note: Tranquil is slightly more formal or literary than peaceful.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: The coastal path passes through some spectacular scenery.
items.note: Spectacular scenery is supported by the answer key as a correction of an unnatural adjective pairing.

items.section: B · Describing scenic views and tourism
items.example: The remote village is well worth visiting despite the long drive.
items.note: Well worth is naturally followed by the -ing form; a lot worth visiting is incorrect.

units.title: Unit 16 — Towns and cities
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 36–37 (PDF pages 40–41).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Travel and the environment · urban life and city descriptions
learningObjectives: Describe city architecture, shopping, streets and atmosphere with natural collocations.
Contrast positive visitor descriptions with terms for decay, poverty, traffic and pollution.
Distinguish near-synonyms such as pricey versus overpriced and inner city versus deprived area.
Use verb–noun and adjective–noun patterns for city routes, urban form and amenities.

items.pt: silhueta urbana; linha do horizonte da cidade
items.example: The new tower has changed the city skyline.
items.note: Skyline is the outline of buildings visible against the sky.

items.example: The old quarter is famous for its narrow cobbled streets.
items.note: Cobbled refers to streets paved with small stones.

items.pt: centro histórico; parte antiga da cidade
items.example: We spent the morning exploring the old town on foot.
items.note: Old town refers to the historic part of a city or town.

items.pt: área de preservação histórica ou ambiental
items.example: Many historic buildings are protected within the conservation area.
items.note: In British usage, a conservation area can be a legally designated district whose character is protected.

items.pt: prédios antigos pitorescos; construções antigas charmosas
items.example: The village centre has several quaint old buildings.
items.note: Quaint is generally positive and suggests attractive, unusual, old-fashioned character.

items.example: The city walls date back to the fifteenth century.
items.note: Use date back to with a period or time in the past, often when describing buildings.

items.pt: lojas sofisticadas; lojas de alto padrão
items.example: The district has upmarket shops selling designer clothes.
items.note: Upmarket suggests expensive goods aimed at wealthier customers.

items.example: We chose a café rather than a pricey restaurant.
items.note: Pricey is relatively informal and often implies a high price, without necessarily poor value.

items.pt: restaurante com preços abusivos; restaurante caro demais para o que oferece
items.example: The overpriced restaurant was nearly empty despite its central location.
items.note: Overpriced means too expensive for its quality or value, unlike merely pricey.

items.example: The set lunch was good value for the quality of the food.
items.note: Good value means worth its cost; good value for money is a common fuller expression.

items.example: The small café has a relaxed atmosphere in the evening.
items.note: A positive description of a comfortable, informal mood or environment.

items.example: We met our friends at a lively bar near the station.
items.note: Lively describes an energetic place with activity and conversation.

items.pt: casa noturna badalada; clube da moda
items.example: A fashionable club opened near the waterfront last month.
items.note: Fashionable means currently popular among people who follow trends.

items.example: We had breakfast at a pavement café overlooking the square.
items.note: A pavement café has outdoor seating along the pavement; British English uses pavement where American English often uses sidewalk.

items.pt: rua repleta de lojas dos dois lados
items.example: The station leads onto a street lined with shops and bakeries.
items.note: Be lined with describes things arranged along the sides of a street.

items.example: The museum is situated on a tree-lined avenue.
items.note: The compound adjective tree-lined describes a road bordered by trees.

items.example: They live in a residential area away from the main shopping streets.
items.note: Residential describes a district primarily used for homes rather than industry or commerce.

items.pt: apartamentos em edifícios altos; prédios residenciais altos
items.example: The neighbourhood has many high-rise flats near the railway.
items.note: High-rise refers to buildings with many storeys; flats is British English for apartments.

items.example: The charity supports families living in the inner city.
items.note: Inner city means the central urban area; it does not automatically mean an unsafe or deprived district.

items.example: Several imposing buildings surround the government square.
items.note: Imposing describes buildings that make a strong impression through size or appearance.

items.pt: área urbana degradada; terreno urbano abandonado
items.example: Years of neglect turned the industrial site into an urban wasteland.
items.note: A strongly negative description of an abandoned or badly deteriorated city area.

items.pt: área perigosa ou de acesso proibido
items.example: The abandoned site became a no-go area after dark.
items.note: A no-go area is somewhere people are advised not to enter, often because of danger or restrictions.

items.example: Residents are demanding action to tackle high crime in the district.
items.note: High is the natural modifier for the level of crime in an area.

items.example: The streets were strewn with litter after the outdoor concert.
items.note: Strewn with means scattered over a surface, typically untidily.

items.pt: edifícios deteriorados; prédios em mau estado
items.example: The council plans to restore several run-down buildings.
items.note: Run-down means in poor condition because of age, neglect or lack of maintenance.

items.example: The programme funds schools in deprived areas of the city.
items.note: Deprived suggests a lack of important resources and opportunities, not merely low property prices.

items.example: Unemployment and poor housing can contribute to serious social problems.
items.note: This phrase refers to difficulties affecting communities or society.

items.example: The new warehouses will be built in an industrial zone outside town.
items.note: Industrial zones are areas assigned mainly to factories and related businesses.

items.pt: cidade muito espalhada; cidade extensa e dispersa
items.example: It can take hours to cross such a sprawling city.
items.note: Sprawling often suggests that an urban area covers a very large space, sometimes inefficiently.

items.pt: trânsito congestionado; carros praticamente encostados uns nos outros
items.example: We were caught in bumper-to-bumper traffic on the ring road.
items.note: Describes extremely dense, slow-moving traffic where vehicles are very close together.

items.pt: gases do escapamento; fumaça dos veículos
items.example: Cyclists complained about exhaust fumes near the tunnel.
items.note: Exhaust fumes are gases released by vehicle engines.

items.pt: volume de tráfego; quantidade de veículos circulando
items.example: The volume of traffic increased after the new bridge opened.
items.note: Volume refers to the amount of traffic, not how loud the traffic sounds.

items.example: The incessant roar of traffic made it difficult to sleep.
items.note: Incessant means continuous; roar vividly suggests loud traffic noise.

items.pt: subúrbios confortáveis; bairros residenciais afastados e bem estruturados
items.example: The family moved to the comfortable suburbs outside the city centre.
items.note: Suburbs are residential districts outside the central urban area; comfortable describes their living conditions.

items.pt: favela de barracos; assentamento de moradias precárias
items.example: The report describes families living in a shanty town without reliable water supplies.
items.note: A shanty town consists of makeshift, poorly built homes; the term may sound stigmatising, so use with care.

items.pt: periferia da cidade; arredores da cidade
items.example: A large distribution centre was built on the outskirts of the city.
items.note: Outskirts are the outer parts of a town or city, not necessarily deprived areas.
